ai-at-work.title: From PGP to Mythos: a brief history of export controls that didn’t stop anyone
ai-at-work.excerpt: For the last 30 years, stopping the flow of cybersecurity-related software has proven to be ineffective. It's unclear why it would work now with Anthropic’s cybersecurity model Mythos.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: The U.S. government has spent three decades trying to restrict exports of encryption and security software, and it basically hasn't worked, yet they're apparently trying the same playbook with Anthropic's new Mythos cybersecurity model. This matters because digital workplace security depends on actual security tools reaching the right hands, and watching governments chase the same failed strategy while real threats move at lightspeed is like watching your IT team patch Windows 95 vulnerabilities. Here's the thing: if you're building workplace security strategy around hoping export controls will somehow magically work this time around, you're already behind.

ai-at-work.dwp_take: The US government forced Anthropic to pull two AI models citing national security risks after researchers found guardrail bypasses, though similar vulnerabilities apparently exist in competitor models too. For digital workplace professionals, this matters because it highlights the messy reality of AI governance at scale, where regulatory decisions can look inconsistent and may drive adoption decisions more than actual security differences. Honestly, banning a product while leaving functionally equivalent alternatives on the market is a masterclass in generating sympathy for the banned company, and Anthropic's PR team is probably uncorking champagne right now.

ai-at-work.title: Mississippi Department of Revenue balances cloud modernization with security-first AI adoption
ai-at-work.excerpt: Public sector organizations are increasingly rethinking how they manage critical infrastructure as demands for always-on digital services and greater operational efficiency continue to grow. As govern
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Mississippi's Department of Revenue moved their infrastructure to the cloud while carefully vetting AI tools to avoid security breaches and maintain public trust. The real story here is that "measured" approach to AI adoption, which is code for "we're not throwing everything at ChatGPT and hoping for the best," and honestly that's the most refreshing government tech decision I've heard all year.

tools-tech.title: Solving an ARD problem in AI: Agentic Resource Discovery
tools-tech.excerpt: Enterprises implementing agentic AI face a challenge: Which tools should they allow their agents to use, where can they be found, and how can they be used safely? A new protocol, Agentic Resource Disc
tools-tech.dwp_take: A new protocol called Agentic Resource Discovery is being developed by major tech companies to help AI agents figure out which tools they can safely access and use across enterprise systems. This matters because digital workplace professionals are going to be managing these AI agents, and right now it's like handing someone the keys to your filing cabinets without a map. If ARD actually standardizes this stuff, it could save teams from the chaos of ad-hoc agent permissions, though I'll believe the standardization part when I see it actually work across competing vendors.

tools-tech.title: US should take 50% stake in major AI firms, says Bernie Sanders
tools-tech.excerpt: With the market capitalization of AI companies soaring, US Senator Bernie Sanders is looking to give the American people a piece of the action. The veteran senator for Vermont has introduced the Ameri
tools-tech.dwp_take: Bernie Sanders wants the US government to own half of America's biggest AI companies through a new sovereign wealth fund. This matters to digital workplace pros because AI is already reshaping how we work, collaborate, and automate tasks, so whoever controls these tools controls your workplace future. Look, I've seen a lot of wild policy proposals in three decades, but getting Congress to agree on anything involving AI and public ownership might take longer than actually developing AGI.

tools-tech.title: OpenAI gets the attention it needs from AI researcher Noam Shazeer

tools-tech.dwp_take: Noam Shazeer, a prominent AI researcher, left Google to join OpenAI, signaling continued brain drain from Big Tech to the AI startup world. For digital workplace leaders, this matters because it shows where serious AI talent sees the future happening and what that means for their own organization's ability to compete for skilled people. The real story here is that Google's massive resources apparently can't keep brilliant people from heading for the door when they think the more interesting work is happening elsewhere, which should worry every large organization trying to hold onto their best people.

tools-tech.title: Google, Microsoft offer specs to help you prove your AI is behaving nicely

tools-tech.dwp_take: Google and Microsoft are joining forces with OpenAI to create the Appia Foundation, which will develop specifications to help companies prove their AI systems are trustworthy and behaving properly. This matters because digital workplace leaders are getting hammered by executives demanding AI governance frameworks, and having actual standards to point to beats making something up on the fly. The real question is whether this foundation will produce anything useful or just become another standards body where everyone nods solemnly before shipping AI systems that still hallucinate in production.

digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company is declaring the traditional marketing funnel obsolete because AI has shifted buyer behavior so dramatically that prospects now arrive at vendor doors already informed and ready to decide. industry-news.title: Android 17 Is Live on Pixel, but Samsung and Other Android Users Still Have to Wait
industry-news.excerpt: Android 17 is rolling out to supported Pixel devices first, while non-Pixel users and IT teams face separate OEM timelines, beta programs, and app-testing considerations. The post Android 17 Is Live o
industry-news.dwp_take: Google's releasing Android 17 to Pixel phones first while everyone else, including Samsung users, gets left waiting for their OEM's separate rollout schedule. This matters because IT teams managing mixed Android environments now face the usual fragmentation nightmare: different devices on different OS versions, different security patches, different capabilities, all at the same time. After three decades watching this play out, I can tell you that "we'll get to your devices eventually" is IT speak for "good luck managing this mess for the next six months."

industry-news.excerpt: Cybernews researchers found an exposed database with 24 billion credential records, raising fresh risks from password reuse and credential stuffing. The post 24B Records Exposed in Massive Leak of Ema
industry-news.dwp_take: A database containing 24 billion credential records got exposed, giving bad actors a massive collection of emails, passwords, and login data to work with.
